title: MillerKing, LLC v. DoNotPay, Inc. — Law Firm's Lanham Act Suit Against the 'Robot Lawyer' Dismissed for Lack of Article III Standing
pub: MillerKing, LLC v. DoNotPay, Inc., No. 3:23-cv-863-NJR (S.D. Ill. Nov. 17, 2023)
author: Chief Judge Nancy J. Rosenstengel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source resolves Article III standing rather than evaluating AI’s task-level capabilities, verification needs, human–AI division of labour or workflow redesign. Its distinction between lawyer-delivered and AI-based services is relevant context, but the court made no merits finding that supports or rejects the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: These allegations are insufficient to establish Article III standing.
While the parties may work in similar industries, the services they provide are different enough that the Court will not infer an injury based on these statements.

kp.k: Subscription AI offered automated legal documents and litigation assistance
kp.d: The opinion recounts complaint allegations, accepted as true for the dismissal motion, that DoNotPay supplied AI-based legal services without being licensed or employing licensed attorneys. Its automatically renewed subscription cost $36 for two months and covered personalized contracts and other documents, traffic-ticket and property-tax assistance, demand letters, court filings and courtroom scripts. These are allegations about the service, not adjudicated findings about its capabilities.
qs: DNP is an online subscription service that uses artificial intelligence to provide a variety of legal services, although it is not licensed to practice law and does not employ licensed attorneys.
Customers pay $36 for two months of service, which is renewed automatically.

Other personalized legal documents DNP offers to generate include independent contractor agreements, non-disclosure agreements, bills of sale, prenuptial agreements, LLC operating agreements, promissory notes, and parenting plans.

kp.k: Reported growth did not establish traditional law-firm displacement
kp.d: The complaint reported approximately 250,000 subscribers and a valuation of about $210 million by June 2021, alongside company claims about parking-ticket and small-claims activity. Browder claimed over 2 million processed cases as of January 2023. The court did not treat this reported growth as evidence of MillerKing's losses: the complaint did not connect users to MillerKing or establish that they would otherwise have hired any law firm.
qs: By June 2021, DNP had “attracted numerous investors, doubled its valuation to about $210 million, and had approximately 250,000 subscribers.”

As of January 2023, Browder claimed that DNP had “processed over 2 million cases” and touted that DNP's “robot lawyer” would soon represent someone in a courtroom by whispering in the person's ear exactly what to say.

For example, while the complaint references the hundreds of thousands of parking ticket cases that DNP claims to have taken on, there is no allegation that those customers originally were clients of MK, had considered hiring MK, or would have sought the advice of any law firm in the first place if not for the representations made by DNP.
Again, the Court will not infer that MK has suffered harm through lost clients just because DNP has gained them.

kp.k: Alleged service failures raised consumer legal-risk concerns
kp.d: The complaint cited poor subscriber reviews, failures to dispute parking tickets, inadequate documents and inaccurate form information. MillerKing alleged that these mistakes could expose subscribers to limitations problems or civil or criminal liability. These reported failures and prospective risks were not independently established by the court; nor did they establish reputational injury to MillerKing.
qs: Several subscribers have posted poor online reviews of DNP due to its failure to perform as advertised.
For example, DNP has failed to dispute parking tickets as requested, has created inadequate legal documents, or has included inaccurate information in its forms.
MK alleges these mistakes could subject DNP's subscribers to statute of limitations issues, or worse, civil or criminal liability.

kp.k: Bar-enforcement threats reportedly halted planned courtroom AI deployment
kp.d: The opinion reports Browder's proposed courtroom use of AI to tell a person what to say, followed by his announcement postponing the plan because of state bar prosecutors' threats. The complaint also reported product removals by the end of January 2023, while other legal offerings continued. The document describes an announced and postponed deployment, not demonstrated courtroom representation.
qs: Shortly thereafter, Browder announced that DNP would postpone its plan to bring AI into the courtroom because of “threats from State Bar prosecutors.”

By the end of January 2023, DNP had removed some products from its website, though it continued to advertise and promote legal products and services including defamation demand letters, divorce certificates, divorce settlement agreements, and numerous other categories of legal services.

kp.k: Lawyer branding prompted advertising and unauthorized-practice claims
kp.d: MillerKing alleged that DoNotPay's representations falsely implied affiliation with licensed attorneys and state-bar approval, and that describing the offering as a robot lawyer or attorney influenced purchases. It also alleged unauthorized practice under the Illinois Attorney Act and Corporation Practice of Law Prohibition Act. These were the plaintiff's legal theories; the standing dismissal did not decide whether the advertising or services were unlawful.
qs: Specifically, MK alleges that (1) it is a direct competitor of DNP and that (2) DNP made numerous representations [1](#footnote_1) that create the false impression that DNP is affiliated with licensed attorneys and that State bar authorities approve of or sponsor DNP's services.
MK claims DNP falsely represented that its legal services and products would be offered by a robot “lawyer” and “attorney,” which likely influenced subscribers’ purchasing decisions.

MK claims DNP has violated the Illinois Attorney Act, 705 ILCS 205/1, and the Corporation Practice of Law Prohibition Act, 705 ILCS 220/1 and 705 ILCS 220/2, by engaging in the practice of law without a license from the Illinois Supreme Court.

kp.k: Court distinguished AI subscriptions from licensed law-firm services
kp.d: For the requested inference of competitive injury, the court rejected MillerKing's argument that overlapping practice areas made the parties direct competitors. It contrasted licensed lawyers' representation, arguments and signed documents with a virtual AI subscription service, concluding that similar industries did not mean identical products. This reasoning concerned the pleaded basis for standing, rather than an empirical assessment of market-wide substitution.
qs: MK is a law firm employing real, licensed attorneys who appear in court before judges, represent clients, make legal arguments, and sign legal documents.
DNP is a web-based company purporting to use AI to provide legal services virtually.
In other words, while the parties participate in similar industries, they are not selling identical products.
Therefore, MK's argument that the parties are “direct competitors” fails, and the Court will not presume a commercial injury for purposes of Article III standing.

kp.k: Competitive and reputational injury required concrete factual allegations
kp.d: The court held that MillerKing had not plausibly alleged diverted clients, lost revenue, additional expenses or diminished goodwill. DoNotPay's alleged customer-service failures were not linked to reputational damage to MillerKing or lawyers generally. The court distinguished statutory Lanham Act requirements from the independent constitutional requirement of concrete injury, rejecting presumed harm from allegedly false statements.
qs: As argued by DNP, MK has not alleged any lost revenue or added expenditures as a result of DNP's conduct.
Nor has it alleged that any client or prospective client has withheld business, has considered withholding business, or has even heard of DNP.

While the complaint asserts that DNP has provided poor customer service at times, leading to adverse legal consequences for DNP's customers, the complaint fails to cite any instance where DNP's failures were imputed to MK specifically or lawyers generally.

Even if the Court were to find that MK (a law firm) is a “direct competitor” of DNP (an AI-based legal subscription service), MK has conflated the injury requirement for a statutory cause of action under the Lanham Act claim with Article III's injury-in-fact requirement, as evidenced by the cases it cites.

kp.k: Standing ruling left service legality unresolved
kp.d: The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for lack of Article III standing. The deficiency extended to the Illinois deceptive-trade-practices and unauthorized-practice claims: MillerKing alleged no particularized unauthorized-practice harm to itself and no sufficiently imminent harm supporting an injunction. The ruling therefore addressed this plaintiff's ability to sue in federal court, not the merits of AI legal-service legality.
qs: MK has not sufficiently alleged any imminent harm that will occur if DNP is not enjoined from its conduct.
The same can be said for MK's claim in Count IV that DNP has engaged in the unauthorized practice of law in Illinois, where MK has alleged no particularized harm to it whatsoever.
For these reasons, the Motion to Dismiss filed by Defendant DoNotPay, Inc. (Doc. 20) is GRANTED and the Complaint (Doc. 1) is DISMISSED without prejudice.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The opinion describes consumer-facing AI automation of legal documents and procedural assistance, contested claims of harm to consumers and law firms, and a narrow judicial finding that this plaintiff had not plausibly alleged competitive injury.
pts.d: Chief Judge Rosenstengel recounts allegations that DoNotPay offered personalized contracts, demand letters, court filings and procedural guidance through an AI subscription service rather than licensed attorneys. These are descriptions of advertised capabilities and complaint allegations, not judicially validated performance findings. The complaint also recounts CEO Joshua Browder's announced plan for AI to whisper courtroom instructions to a user and its subsequent postponement. MillerKing alleges that inadequate documents, inaccurate forms and failed services could expose subscribers to missed limitations periods or liability, and that DoNotPay diverts clients and diminishes law firms' goodwill. The judge holds that MillerKing provided insufficient factual allegations of those injuries. For purposes of the standing argument, she distinguishes a licensed law firm's representation from a web-based AI service and declines to infer commercial injury from product overlap or DoNotPay's growth. This is not a finding that AI cannot compete with lawyers, nor a merits ruling validating DoNotPay's advertising or deciding whether it engaged in unauthorized practice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The service and market claims rest on complaint allegations, advertising, reported company statements and subscriber reviews; the judicial conclusion rests on pleading deficiencies and standing precedents.
pts.d: The court expressly accepts well-pleaded complaint facts as true for this facial jurisdictional challenge. The complaint cites DoNotPay's website, its claimed parking-ticket outcomes, subscriber and valuation figures, Browder's statements about case volumes, and poor online reviews. Reported figures include $4 million in overturned parking fines, approximately 250,000 subscribers and a valuation of about $210 million by June 2021, more than 1,000 small-claims lawsuits against one company in 42 states reported a year later, and over 2 million processed cases claimed in January 2023. These are not independent measurements of AI accuracy, legal quality or displacement. The judge identifies the absence of allegations of MillerKing's lost revenue, added expenditure, identifiable diverted clients or reputational damage. Standing authorities support the requirement of a concrete, particularized injury rather than an inference from the defendant's commercial success.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns services and growth claims through early 2023 and a November 17, 2023 pleading-stage decision; the proposed courtroom deployment was postponed.
pts.d: Growth claims refer to June 2021, a statement a year later, and January 2023. Browder's courtroom plan was prospective in January 2023 and was reportedly postponed shortly afterward because of threats from State Bar prosecutors. Some products were removed by the end of January 2023, while other legal offerings remained advertised. The court's conclusions are limited to the sufficiency of MillerKing's complaint: damages-related standing required concrete injury, and injunctive standing required sufficiently imminent and substantial future harm. The complaint was dismissed without prejudice with leave to amend by December 18, 2023. The document supplies no later outcome or general forecast for AI's effect on legal employment or market share.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The described effects concern subscribers seeking routine legal help, small law firms alleging overlapping services, and the public and judicial system alleged to be exposed to unlicensed legal work.
pts.d: Consumers were offered automatically renewed subscriptions costing $36 for two months for matters including parking and traffic tickets, small claims, leases, family-related documents, trusts and contracts. The advertised benefit was automated document preparation and help navigating disputes; MillerKing alleged failures and possible legal consequences. MillerKing is a six-attorney firm that sought to represent all US law firms, with an Illinois subclass, and emphasized potential harm to small firms with overlapping offerings. The judge found no sufficiently pleaded particularized injury to MillerKing. She also noted the absence of allegations that DoNotPay's parking-ticket customers would otherwise have hired MillerKing or any law firm, leaving substitution for paid legal representation unestablished. The complaint alleged broader harm to citizens and the judicial system, but those allegations did not establish this firm's standing.
